title: Aeroflot 6246
summary: A Tupolev Tu-134A registered CCCP-65951 with 71 persons aboard caught fire shortly after takeoff on a scheduled domestic flight from Tyumen to Volgograd with a stop at Ufa. At 2:24 PM local time the aircraft took off, reaching 10,600 meters at 2:45. At 2:48 PM a fire alarm sounded in the auxiliary power unit, and the flight mechanic confirmed the presence of fire in the rear baggage compartment. The fire was caused by a short circuit in electrical wiring in the area of frames 48-50 on the left side of the aircraft. Faced with dense fog near the destination airport, the crew force-landed in a snow-covered field near Pervouralsk. The aircraft landed with gear down, all three landing gear legs broke, and the aircraft bounced multiple times before the right wing tore off and the fuselage flipped, killing 27 people.
probable_cause: A short circuit in electrical wiring caused a breakdown in insulation in the area of frames 48-50 on the left side of the aircraft in the rear baggage compartment, igniting a fire that spread and consumed electrical power systems.

title: SANSA 32
summary: SANSA Flight 32 took off from Juan Santamaria at 08:25 local time and was cleared to climb to 5500 feet. Soon after, the crew received instructions to climb to 8500 feet. Midway through the climb, the aircraft flew into Cerro Cedral at 7200 feet, killing all 23 on board. The investigation found the main cause was failure to comply with the proposed flight plan, which led the aircraft to fly under IMC conditions instead of VFR ones.

title: Avianca 052
summary: Avianca Flight 052 ran out of fuel after three holding patterns and a failed landing attempt at JFK, crashing onto a hillside in Cove Neck on Long Island. Due to poor communication and inadequate fuel management, the flight became critically low on fuel but controllers did not recognize the emergency because pilots failed to use the word 'emergency'. The crew's failure to properly declare a fuel emergency and inadequate traffic flow management by the FAA contributed to the accident.
probable_cause: The flight crew failed to properly declare a fuel emergency and inadequately managed the fuel load. Poor communication between crew and controllers and lack of standardized terminology for emergency fuel states contributed.

title: Indian Airlines 605
summary: Indian Airlines Flight 605, an Airbus A320, crashed onto a golf course near Bangalore Airport on February 14, 1990 while attempting to land. The crew selected the 'Open descent' automation mode rather than 'Glideslope capture', causing the aircraft to descend well below the correct flight path. Despite radio altitude call-outs warning of the descent, the crew failed to advance throttles or correct the trajectory in time.
probable_cause: The crew selected the incorrect flight control mode ('Open descent/flight idle' rather than 'Glideslope capture'), which allowed the aircraft to sink far below the correct approach path. The crew were unaware of their dangerously low position and reacted too late to the altitude call-outs.

title: Widerøe 839

aircraft.type: de Havilland Canada DHC-6-300 Twin Otter

summary: Widerøe Flight 839, a scheduled DHC-6 flight departing Værøy Airport, encountered extreme wind conditions that exceeded the aircraft's structural limits. The crew took off with wind speeds of 57 knots, exceeding the Twin Otter's 50-knot ground wind limit. Strong winds alternating from multiple directions caused cracks to develop in the tail rudder and tailplane, rendering the aircraft uncontrollable. The aircraft crashed into the water 63 seconds after takeoff, with control lost during the final 8 seconds.
probable_cause: The Norwegian Accident Investigation Board concluded that the crew should not have taken off with winds above tolerance levels. Strong winds alternating on both sides of the tail structure due to shifting winds caused cracks in the rudder and tailplane, leading to loss of control and water impact. Although the aircraft was under control for the first 55 seconds of flight, structural failure during the final 8 seconds made recovery impossible.

title: Philippine Airlines 143
summary: A Boeing 737-300 suffered an explosion in the center wing fuel tank on May 11, 1990 at Manila airport. Air temperature was approximately 35°C and the air conditioning packs had run for 30 to 45 minutes before pushback. The center wing fuel tank contained vapors that ignited due to damaged wiring from logo lights installed after delivery. The aircraft was consumed by fire in as little as four minutes. 112 survivors escaped via emergency exits.

title: British Airways 5390
summary: A BAC One-Eleven Series 528FL operating British Airways Flight 5390 suffered explosive decompression on 10 June 1990 at 17,300 feet near Didcot, England. An improperly installed windscreen panel separated from its frame, ejecting the captain partially from the aircraft. He was held in place through the window frame for 20 minutes until first officer Aitchison successfully landed the aircraft at Southampton. All 92 occupants survived.
probable_cause: Improper windscreen installation: 84 of 90 screws were undersized by 0.026 inches and six were 0.1 inch too short, unable to withstand the air pressure difference. The fitted-from-outside windscreen type allowed cabin pressure to dislodge rather than hold it. Previous maintenance had also used incorrect screws on a like-for-like basis without consulting documentation.

title: 1990 Guangzhou Baiyun airport collisions
summary: On 2 October 1990, a hijacked Boeing 737-200 operating Xiamen Airlines Flight 8301 collided with two other aircraft at Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport while attempting to land. The hijacked aircraft struck parked China Southwest Airlines Flight 4305, a Boeing 707, first, then collided with CAAC Flight 3523, a Boeing 757 waiting to take off, flipping onto its back. A total of 128 people were killed, including seven of nine crew members and 75 of 93 passengers on Flight 8301 and 46 of 110 passengers on Flight 3523, making the incident the deadliest aircraft hijacking prior to the September 11 attacks.

title: Alitalia 404
summary: Alitalia Flight 404, a DC-9, was on approach to Zurich Airport when the captain's instrument landing system display malfunctioned due to a faulty NAV receiver, incorrectly indicating the aircraft was 1,000 feet higher than its actual altitude. The first officer's ILS display was working correctly and showed the dangerously low approach. Without thoroughly examining which value was correct, the captain decided to ignore the first officer and aborted the first officer's go-around attempt. The aircraft subsequently struck Stadlerberg Mountain at 1,660 feet, killing all 46 occupants. The faulty receiver also prevented the autopilot and ground proximity warning system from receiving proper signals.
probable_cause: A short circuit in the captain's NAV receiver caused it to display incorrect altitude information while preventing the autopilot and GPWS from functioning. The captain's failure to respond to the first officer's warnings and attempt to override the go-around initiated by the first officer, combined with inadequate crew resource management, resulted in controlled flight into terrain.

title: Tu-154M crash
summary: A Tu-154M operated by Aeroflot was performing a cargo flight from Basel to Moscow loaded with 1,217 boxes of Winston cigarettes. The cargo was improperly stowed between seats, in aisles, and in the galley, blocking crew access to the rear fuselage. At 15:08 over Polish airspace, the flight deck detected smoke in the cabin with no fire alarm activating. The crew reported the emergency to Prague Airport and requested landing. The inspector ordered emergency descent but pilots initiated a normal descent instead. Smoke intensified and smoke entered the cockpit, disorienting the crew. The aircraft crash-landed successfully in a field near Dubenec with all 6 crew members surviving but injured.
probable_cause: In-flight fire likely originating from an electric stove in the right galley activated by vibrations from cigarette boxes. Improper cargo loading blocked access to the fire source. The crew's failure to execute emergency descent at the proper rate delayed effective response.
